beats.intro: Chapter seven, lesson three. Selective permeability, diffusion, and osmosis. [[dye]]Drop a speck of dye into a glass of water, and without any stirring, the color slowly spreads until the whole glass looks the same. [[cell]]A cell lives by the same rules, with one big difference. It is wrapped in a membrane that decides what may pass. [[patch]]Here is our patch of membrane from the last two lessons. [[lit]]Today the lipid bilayer and the transport proteins are lit. We ask what gets across, how, and why.
beats.bilayer: Concept seven point two. A cell must exchange materials with its surroundings, and the plasma membrane controls that traffic. [[sel]]The membrane is selectively permeable. It lets some substances cross more easily than others. [[nonpolar]]Start with hydrophobic, or nonpolar, molecules, like hydrocarbons. Oxygen and carbon dioxide are small nonpolar molecules too. They dissolve in the oily core of the bilayer, so they cross rapidly. [[polar]]Polar molecules, such as sugars, do not cross the membrane easily. A sugar is hydrophilic, and the core is made of hydrophobic tails, so a sugar has nowhere comfortable to go. [[ions]]Charged ions have an even harder time. That point goes a little beyond the slides, but it follows the same rule: an ion is wrapped in water, and that wrapping cannot slip into the oil. [[border]]Think of a border checkpoint. Some travelers walk straight through. Everyone else needs a gate.
beats.proteins: So how do hydrophilic substances get across? [[tp]]Through transport proteins, which span the membrane. [[channel]]A channel protein has a hydrophilic channel, a tunnel, that certain molecules or ions use to cross. [[aqua]]One special channel is the aquaporin, a tunnel for water. [[carrier]]A carrier protein works differently. It binds a molecule, changes shape, and shuttles the molecule across. [[specific]]And each transport protein is specific for the substance it moves. A protein that carries glucose does not carry sodium. [[later]]Lesson five studies how these proteins work. For now, remember two pictures: a tunnel, and a shape change.
beats.q1: Quick check. Which of these can cross the bare bilayer on its own?
beats.diffusion: Concept seven point three. Passive transport is diffusion across a membrane, with no energy investment from the cell. [[spread]]Diffusion is the tendency of molecules to spread out evenly into the available space. Here is a box split by a membrane. Dye on the left, none on the right. [[random]]Every single molecule moves at random. None of them knows where it is going. [[net]]But there are more dye molecules on the left, so more cross from left to right than from right to left. The population shows net movement to the right, from many random steps. [[eq]]In the end the dye is spread evenly. This is dynamic equilibrium. As many molecules cross one way as the other. They never stop moving. It is the net movement that stops. [[two]]Now add a second dye, in purple. [[indep]]Each solute follows its own gradient. Orange drifts right, purple drifts left, and neither cares about the other. The blue background is the water, the solvent.
beats.gradient: [[grad]]The difference in a substance's concentration from one area to another is its concentration gradient. [[down]]Substances diffuse down their gradient, from where they are crowded to where they are sparse, and no work is needed to move them that way. Like a ball rolling downhill. [[passive]]That is why diffusion across a membrane is called passive transport. The cell spends no energy. [[through]]A nonpolar molecule can go straight through the bilayer. A polar one can use a transport protein. Either way, it is still going downhill.
beats.osmosis: Now water. [[osm]]Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane. [[tube]]Here is a U shaped tube with a membrane across the bottom. The membrane lets water through, but not sugar. The left arm has a little sugar. The right arm has more. [[dir]]Water moves from the region of lower solute concentration, to the region of higher solute concentration. So water crosses toward the sugar side. [[inset]]Zoom into the membrane. Water molecules cross both ways, but more cross toward the sugar. [[why]]Sugar molecules crowd in among the water and hold on to some of it, so there are fewer free water molecules on the sugar side to cross back. [[rise]]As water enters, the sugar side is diluted and its column rises. It ends higher, not level, because the weight of the taller column pushes back.
beats.q2: Quick check. Water on both sides, more sugar on the right. Which way does the water move?
beats.example: Let's meet four travelers at the membrane. [[o2]]Oxygen is small and nonpolar. It dissolves in the bilayer and diffuses straight in, down its gradient, with no energy. [[glu]]Glucose is polar. It cannot cross the bare bilayer, so it needs a carrier protein, and it still moves downhill. [[na]]A sodium ion is charged. It needs a channel, a hydrophilic tunnel. [[h2o]]Water crosses by osmosis, a little through the bilayer, and much faster through aquaporins, toward the side with more solute. [[all]]Four travelers, three kinds of route, and the same rule: nothing here costs the cell energy.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]The membrane is selectively permeable. Nonpolar molecules cross the bilayer rapidly. Polar molecules and ions need transport proteins, channels or carriers. [[w2]]Diffusion is net movement down a concentration gradient, from random motion, ending in dynamic equilibrium. [[w3]]Moving down a gradient is passive transport, and it costs no energy. [[w4]]Osmosis is the diffusion of water, toward the higher solute concentration. [[end]]Now try the practice.
